cards.q: What is secure management?
cards.a: Secure management protects the interfaces and protocols used to administer network devices, ensuring management traffic is encrypted, authenticated, authorized, restricted to trusted sources, and audited/logged, separated from user traffic where appropriate.

cards.q: What are the preferred secure management choices?
cards.a: SSH instead of Telnet, HTTPS instead of HTTP, SNMPv3 instead of SNMPv1/v2c, and SCP instead of TFTP/FTP.

cards.q: What are the three device planes and their typical protections?
cards.a: Data plane (forwards user traffic; ACLs/infrastructure security), control plane (routing/control protocols; CoPP), and management plane (device administration; SSH, HTTPS, AAA, ACLs, SNMPv3).

cards.q: What is the key distinction between CoPP and secure management?
cards.a: CoPP protects the control plane from excessive traffic destined for the device CPU; secure management protects administrative access to the device.

cards.q: Why is SSH preferred over Telnet for CLI management?
cards.a: SSH (port 22) encrypts the management session and protects credentials/commands from clear-text transmission; Telnet (port 23) is unencrypted.

cards.q: What command enables HTTPS, and does it automatically disable HTTP?
cards.a: 'ip http secure-server' enables HTTPS; it does not automatically disable plain HTTP, which must be disabled with 'no ip http server' separately.

cards.q: How do SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3 differ in security?
cards.a: SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c use community strings with no encryption; SNMPv3 provides authentication and optional privacy/encryption.

cards.q: What are the three SNMPv3 security levels?
cards.a: noAuthNoPriv (no auth, no encryption), authNoPriv (authentication, no encryption), and authPriv (authentication and encryption).

cards.q: Which SNMPv3 security level is the strongest?
cards.a: authPriv, which provides both authentication and privacy/encryption.

cards.q: What is the preferred Cisco secure file transfer, and why?
cards.a: SCP, because it is SSH-based encrypted transfer; it is preferred over TFTP/FTP for transferring IOS images and configuration files.

cards.q: What per-line settings secure a VTY configuration?
cards.a: transport input ssh (prevents Telnet), access-class 99 in (restricts source addresses), login local (uses local username database), and exec-timeout 5 0 (disconnects idle sessions).

cards.q: What does 'access-class' on a VTY line control?
cards.a: It controls which source addresses can access the management line; it is different from an interface ACL used to filter normal transit traffic.

cards.q: What AAA functions support secure management?
cards.a: Authentication (who are you?), authorization (what can you do?), and accounting (what management activity was recorded); configuring authentication alone does not automatically provide command accounting.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a local fallback authentication account?
cards.a: Centralized AAA servers may become unavailable, so a local fallback account with 'aaa authentication login DEFAULT group tacacs+ local' attempts TACACS+ first and uses local if the configured AAA method permits fallback.

cards.q: What is a dedicated management VLAN?
cards.a: A management VLAN separates device-management traffic from normal user VLANs, reducing exposure, simplifying management ACLs, and providing centralized management policy; it is logical isolation, not complete physical isolation.

cards.q: What is out-of-band (OOB) management and its advantages?
cards.a: OOB management uses a separate management network from the production/data network, remaining reachable even when the production network has problems and providing stronger isolation than a management VLAN.

cards.q: How do management ACLs restrict access?
cards.a: They allow only trusted administrative networks (e.g., 'ip access-list standard MGMT permit 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 deny any'), applied to VTY with 'access-class MGMT in' and to HTTP/HTTPS with 'ip http access-class MGMT in'.

cards.q: How does secure management differ from device hardening?
cards.a: Device hardening reduces the overall attack surface of the device (disable services, secure console/AUX, passwords); secure management protects how administrators manage the device (SSH/HTTPS/SNMPv3, AAA, management ACLs, management VLAN/OOB).

cards.q: What verification commands are used for secure management?
cards.a: show ip ssh, show ssh, show line, show running-config | section line vty, show ip http server status, show access-lists, show running-config | section aaa, and show running-config | section snmp.

cards.q: What is the difference between a management VLAN and OOB management?
cards.a: A management VLAN provides logical separation within the network; OOB management uses a separate management path/network and generally provides stronger isolation, remaining available when the production network is unavailable.

cards.q: If HTTP is still available after enabling HTTPS, what is the cause and fix?
cards.a: Enabling 'ip http secure-server' does not disable the plain HTTP server; fix by also configuring 'no ip http server'.
